papers.title: Parallel Repetition for k-Player XOR Games
papers.abstract: In a $k$-XOR game $\Psi$ over $\mathbb{F}_p$, a verifier samples challenges $(x_1,\ldots,x_k)\sim\mu$ where $\mu$ is a distribution over $\Sigma_1\times\ldots\times \Sigma_k$, sends $x_i$ to player $i$ and receives an answer $f_i(x_i)\in\mathbb{F}_p$, and accepts if and only if $f_1(x_1)+\ldots+f_k(x_k)=t(x_1,\ldots,x_k)$, where $t\colon \Sigma_1\times\ldots\times \Sigma_k\to\mathbb{F}_p$ is a fixed map. We show that if $\Psi$ has value strictly less than $1$, then the value of the $n$-fold repeated game $\Psi^{\otimes n}$ is at most $2^{-cn}$ where $c = c(\Psi)>0$ is a fixed constant. This extends a previous result of [Bhangale-Braverman-Khot-Liu-Minzer] showing exponential decay for some $3$-XOR games. Our proof uses a relaxation of the value of games studied in the quantum setting, called the commuting value of a game. We show a transformation that maps a $k$-player game $\Psi$ with value strictly less than $1$ to a $2k$-player game $\Psi'$ with commuting value less than $1$, such that $\mathsf{val}(\Psi^{\otimes n})\leq \mathsf{val}((\Psi')^{\otimes n})$. We prove that $\mathsf{val}(\Psi')<1$ has a direct proof using nothing more than the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality, which we are able to tensorize to get that $\mathsf{val}((\Psi')^{\otimes n})$ vanishes exponentially fast in $n$.

papers.title: No Perfect Randomized Composition
papers.abstract: Does computing a composition of total Boolean functions require the product of the randomized query complexities of its factors? We give a negative answer. There are families of total functions $f,g$ such that $R(f\circ g) =\Theta\!\left(\frac1{\log R(g)}\right)R(f)R(g)$ This result requires first separating linearized query complexity $\LR$, as well as noisy randomized query complexity $noisyR$, from standard randomized query complexity $R$. Both constructions essentially come from totalizing existing partial function separations, albeit via different techniques. By adapting these techniques, we also construct total functions separating every adjacent pair in the chain from sabotage $RS$, max-conflict $\bar{\chi}$, and linearised query complexity $LR$. We show that AND-of-ORs separates conflict $\chi$ from max-conflict $\bar{\chi}$ complexity and makes conflict and sabotage incomparable. Finally, randomized complexity can be smaller than its composition limit $R^*$ by the maximal factor $\Theta(\log R)$. The total--total composition separation is also formalized in Lean.

papers.title: Near-Quadratic Time Multivariate Polynomial Interpolation
papers.abstract: Let $\F$ be a finite field. Given $N$ distinct points $\bm{\alpha}_1,\ldots,\bm{\alpha}_N \in \F^m$ and associated values $\beta_1,\ldots,\beta_N \in \F$, we study the problem of computing an $m$-variate polynomial $f(\vy) \in \F[\vy]$ of individual degree less than $d$, with $d^m \ge N$, that satisfies $f(\bm{\alpha}_i)=\beta_i$ for all $i\in[N]$, whenever such an $f$ exists. This is known as the\textit{ multivariate polynomial interpolation} problem. In this work, given $N=d^m$, we present a deterministic algorithm for multivariate polynomial interpolation over an arbitrary finite field $\F$ that runs in near-quadratic time $N^{2+o(1)}\poly(m,d,\log|\F|)$, assuming $d$ is $\omega(1)$. This bound holds whenever the associated \emph{multivariate Vandermonde} matrix is nonsingular, has constant co-rank, or admits some special structure. In the general case, we give a randomized Las Vegas algorithm attaining the same near-quadratic running time, provided the finite field is sufficiently large and $d$ grows similar to the previous case. Unlike other multivariate interpolation strategies, we do not assume black-box access to the polynomial. In particular, we are not permitted to query arbitrary input points to obtain their evaluations. Our interpolation result follows by combining Wiedemann's classical approach~\cite{w86} for solving sparse linear systems with known bounds for fast \emph{multivariate multipoint evaluation} over finite fields~\cite{umans08, KU11, BGKM23, BGGKU24}. Specifically, our deterministic interpolation strategy relies on a deterministic variant of Wiedemann's approach, which is more commonly used in the randomized setting.

papers.title: Dissipation Bounds and Hardness in Globally Asymptotically Stable Quadratic Systems
papers.abstract: Approximating the maximum retained energy fraction in globally asymptotically stable quadratic systems of growing dimension is NP-hard at every fixed positive additive error below $1/2$, even when strict quartic Lyapunov functions and strictness proofs are constructed in polynomial time and included in the input. Polynomial-factor approximation is also NP-hard for the least dissipated fraction, energy-halving time and structured coefficient distance to loss of asymptotic stability. For a partially damped family, minimum unit-sphere coupling norm equals that distance, with two-sided inverse-square halving-time bounds at distances in $(0,1/2]$ and explicit coefficient factors. Additive hardness persists under structured coefficient perturbations and direct damping, even with global exponential stability, a strict quadratic Lyapunov function and a Hurwitz Jacobian.

papers.title: NP-Completeness and ETH-Based Additive Inapproximability of Deterministic Communication Complexity via Relaxed Interlacing
papers.abstract: How difficult is it to find an efficient communication protocol when the entire truth table of the function is given? We give a unified interlacing proof of NP-completeness for exact optimisation and of hardness of approximation. Assuming the Exponential Time Hypothesis, there is a computable, nondecreasing additive error allowance tending to infinity for which approximation is impossible in polynomial time. The proof uses interlacing, which asks the players to solve one problem selected by Alice from a collection of inputs held by Bob. For suitable matrices, a short protocol must reveal enough of Alice's selection to encode a solution to a combinatorial problem. This produces a one-bit communication gap in a polynomial-size matrix and proves exact hardness. Repeating the construction is harder: earlier messages can remove the inputs on which a later lower bound depends. Restriction bounds that survive the construction make the one-bit gain repeatable. A smaller, balanced family of interlaced columns controls the truth-table size. For every fixed number of applications, the construction takes subexponential time in the source length. This rules out every fixed additive error under ETH. A general computability argument then yields the stated unbounded allowance.

papers.title: A Simple Algebraic Proof of the PCP Theorem
papers.abstract: We give the simplest known algebraic proof of the PCP theorem, involving only ingredients like code concatenation, polynomial interpolation, and polynomial multiplication. Specifically, we prove that graph 3-coloring has a polynomial-sized proof that can be verified by a verifier tossing logarithmically many coins and querying a constant number of bits in the proof. In particular, our proof does not involve any PCP compositions; notably, it does not invoke the NP-completeness of any fixed problem, such as SAT or 3-coloring, in the construction of the verifier. The main innovation in our work is a clean, coding theoretic, way to encode univariate polynomials that allows us to implement ``low-degree testing'' using just a constant number of bits of queries. Insights from recent attempts to simplify the PCP proof by the authors (STOC 2026) and Goldreich (ECCC 2025) allow us to observe that low-degree was the key bottleneck in converting previous algebraic constructions of the PCP verifier into a constant query PCP. Thus, by overcoming this bottleneck, we get the full PCP verifier using elementary and self-contained steps. As concrete support for the claimed simplicity, we include the full pseudocode of the PCP verifier, assuming finite field arithmetic, and a full description of the completeness (aka ``honest'') prover, assuming multivariate polynomial arithmetic including interpolation and evaluation, that fit in about a page each.

papers.title: An Optimal Gap-Majority Lemma for Bounded-Round Communication
papers.abstract: Recent work of Sawettamalya and Yu (FOCS 2026) initiated the study of \emph{gap-majority} composition in randomized communication. They showed that if computing a $\{\pm 1\}$-valued function $f$ in $r$ rounds requires $I$ bits of information, then distinguishing whether $\sum_{i=1}^n f(X_i,Y_i)$ is at least $0.01\sqrt{n}$ or at most $-0.01\sqrt{n}$ in $r$ rounds requires $n \cdot (I-O(\log n))$ bits of information. They also conjectured that the $O(\log n)$-additive ``loss'' can be further reduced to $O(1)$. In this note, we show that a minor adaptation of their approach, together with a more refined analysis, achieves the conjectured $O(1)$ loss, establishing a gap-majority lemma for bounded-round communication that is optimal up to constant factors.
